lesson.title: Two Golden Rules: How an Ideal Op-Amp Simplifies Everything
lesson.summary: An operational amplifier is a high gain differential amplifier that, wired with negative feedback, behaves as if it obeys two remarkably simple golden rules, turning circuit analysis that would otherwise need calculus into basic algebra.
lesson.body:
An operational amplifier, or op-amp, is an integrated circuit built to amplify the voltage difference between its two input terminals by an enormous factor, often 100,000 or more. Its schematic symbol is a triangle with two inputs on the flat side, marked with a plus for the noninverting input and a minus for the inverting input, and a single output at the triangle's point, alongside power supply pins that are often left off simplified schematics. Recognizing that triangle and its labeled terminals is the first step toward reading any op-amp circuit.

Real op-amps are complicated, but treating them as ideal makes hand analysis remarkably clean, and the approximation is close enough for most introductory work. An ideal op-amp is assumed to have infinite open loop voltage gain, infinite input impedance, and zero output impedance. Combined with negative feedback, a connection that routes some of the output back into the inverting input, these assumptions collapse into two golden rules: first, no current flows into either input terminal, because input impedance is infinite; second, the voltage difference between the two input terminals is zero, V+ = V-, a condition called a virtual short, because the gain is so large that any nonzero input difference would try to drive the output to an impossible voltage.

Consider the classic inverting amplifier: the noninverting input is grounded directly, so V+ = 0 V. The signal Vin = 0.5 V connects through an input resistor Rin = 1 kilohm to the inverting input, and a feedback resistor Rf = 10 kilohms connects from the output back to that same inverting input. By the second golden rule, V- = V+ = 0 V, even though V- is not physically wired to ground, a condition engineers call a virtual ground.

By the first golden rule, no current flows into the inverting input itself, so every bit of current entering through Rin must exit through Rf instead. The current through Rin is I = (Vin - V-)/Rin = (0.5 - 0)/1000 = 0.0005 A, or 0.5 mA. That same 0.5 mA flows through Rf, producing a voltage drop of I times Rf = 0.0005 times 10,000 = 5 V across it. Since that drop goes from the virtual ground node down to the output, Vout = V- - I times Rf = 0 - 5 = -5 V. This matches the standard inverting amplifier formula, Vout = -(Rf/Rin) times Vin = -(10,000/1,000) times 0.5 = -10 times 0.5 = -5 V exactly.

Every step of that calculation leaned on ideas from earlier chapters: current defined as charge flow through a resistor via Ohm's law, voltage defined as the potential difference driving that current, and the schematic symbol conventions needed just to identify which terminal is inverting, which is noninverting, and where the feedback path connects. The op-amp does not introduce new physics so much as it introduces a new and extremely useful set of constraints, the two golden rules, that make circuits built around it solvable with nothing more than the algebra you already have.
